properties.id: Father's Work Ethic and Duty Foundation
properties.description: Father provided foundational influence through 'work ethic, sense of duty' - establishing core values around commitment and responsibility.

properties.id: Mother's Stoicism and Introvert Leadership Model
properties.description: Mother demonstrated 'stoicism and logic to some extent, and how you don't have to be an extrovert, and yet, people are still attracted to you.' This provided a model for non-extroverted leadership and influence.

Limited boss 'did a great job of balancing work and family. Even while he traveled internationally, he worked really hard at it' - demonstrating that high-level professional success can coexist with family commitment.
Integrate different but complementary parental influences - father's work ethic/duty with mother's stoic logic and introvert leadership model.
properties.context: Personal development where foundational family influences provide complementary strengths for professional effectiveness.

properties.description: Learn from professional role models who demonstrate excellence in areas you value, accepting their standards as aspirational even when knowing you may not achieve their level.
properties.context: Professional development where observing excellence in others provides both inspiration and realistic self-assessment.

properties.content: Dan's father provided 'work ethic, sense of duty' while his mother demonstrated 'stoicism and logic to some extent, and how you don't have to be an extrovert, and yet, people are still attracted to you.' These combined influences shaped both his work approach and leadership style.

properties.id: Limited Boss as Work-Life Balance Model
properties.content: Dan's boss at The Limited 'did a great job of balancing work and family. Even while he traveled internationally, he worked really hard at it.' This boss also 'remains the most organized person I've ever met at a level that I am comfortable with now that I will not achieve' - providing both an aspirational model and realistic self-assessment.

properties.description: Effective collaboration requires evaluating 'that person's arguments based on how well you understand their thinking style.' Some people 'go off very quickly' requiring processing adjustments, while others 'literally need to go away and then come back.' This personalized approach is 'part of the orchestration.'

Emotional intelligence manifests 'through the give and take of the collaborative process' where the focus is on 'knowing that they're free to say whatever is on their mind as we try to figure out a solution to the crisis.'
Recognizing when 'an answer is not necessarily what's needed right now because we don't have enough information,' even when 'they may be coming for an answer.'

Adjust collaboration approach based on individual thinking styles - account for those who 'go off very quickly' by processing their input differently, and allow space for those who need time to process.
properties.context: Team collaboration where you know individual team members' cognitive patterns and can adapt your interaction style accordingly.

properties.description: Resist the pressure to provide immediate answers when insufficient information exists, instead creating space for comprehensive information gathering through collaborative exchange.
properties.context: Crisis situations where team members expect immediate answers but the situation requires more data collection first.

properties.content: Dan identifies collaboration as having three components: ideas, information, and personalized evaluation based on understanding each person's thinking style. This includes accommodating those who 'go off very quickly' and allowing others who 'literally need to go away and then come back' to process.

properties.description: Drucker 'never let go of the human element of anything that he did, and he still doesn't seem to get very much credit for that' - emphasizing the importance of maintaining human considerations in business analysis.
'He focused on the real because what I learned from him was what's the real?' This represents looking beyond surface appearances to understand underlying drivers and actual customer needs.

Drucker's 'ability to look into the future' demonstrated through writing 'an article about department stores in the seventies, telling us why they're not going to survive' by understanding real underlying changes rather than surface trends.

properties.id: Real Issue Recognition Over Surface Focus
properties.description: Department stores 'kept focusing on fashion' while 'everything became about time' due to changing demographics. 'Target and Costco came because they addressed the real issue of time' rather than the perceived issue of fashion.
Look beyond what organizations think their value proposition is to understand what customers actually need, particularly when underlying conditions change.
properties.context: Business analysis where organizations may be focused on historical strengths that no longer address current customer realities.

properties.description: Understand how fundamental demographic shifts (like women entering workforce) create new 'real' customer needs that may conflict with traditional business models.
properties.context: Strategic planning where long-term societal changes require businesses to adapt their core value propositions.

properties.content: Dan admires Drucker's predictive ability, citing how he wrote 'an article about department stores in the seventies, telling us why they're not going to survive.' Drucker understood that department stores originally offered 'a different experience for each class' but failed to adapt when 'everything became about time' due to more women entering the workforce. While department stores 'kept focusing on fashion,' Target and Costco succeeded because 'they addressed the real issue of time.'

Dan values Drucker not primarily for knowledge worker concepts but because Drucker 'never let go of the human element of anything that he did, and he still doesn't seem to get very much credit for that.' From Drucker, Dan learned to focus on 'what's the real' - understanding underlying human needs rather than surface business assumptions.

properties.description: 'I still admire Lincoln. I just can't figure it out. I just love reading or hearing stories about even the "Team of Rivals" and the skill required to manage that cabinet and the Civil War and everything is just phenomenal.' Lincoln represents complex leadership under extreme pressure.

'I don't believe in any management tool or fed. Whereas maybe ten years ago I would have like this like we got to do the balanced scorecard or you know what, whatever.' Evolution away from standardized management approaches.

'The best plan is the plan that starts with a recognition of the owner's strengths and weaknesses and then you just borrow. You just borrow and put something together that fits because it has to feel like theirs.'
'If it always feels like someone else's, they do it for a year and then they quit all the time.' Solutions must feel authentic to the person implementing them for long-term success.
Move away from believing in standardized management tools and approaches in favor of customized solutions based on individual leader characteristics.
properties.context: Consulting evolution where experience shows that one-size-fits-all management approaches fail when they don't align with leader personality and strengths.

properties.description: Create solutions that 'feel like theirs' to the owner by starting with their strengths and weaknesses, then borrowing elements that fit their style.
properties.context: Business consulting where sustainability requires solutions that align with the owner's natural operating style rather than imposed best practices.

properties.content: Dan maintains deep admiration for Lincoln, particularly 'the skill required to manage that cabinet and the Civil War and everything is just phenomenal.' He references 'Team of Rivals' and finds Lincoln's complex leadership under extreme pressure continuously fascinating, though he admits 'I just can't figure it out.'

Dan describes moving away from management fads: 'I don't believe in any management tool or fed. Whereas maybe ten years ago I would have like this like we got to do the balanced scorecard.' He now believes 'the best plan is the plan that starts with a recognition of the owner's strengths and weaknesses' because if solutions 'always feels like someone else's, they do it for a year and then they quit.'

properties.description: 'I just don't think I read. I don't even try to recall as much as if it was a good experience. Well, then I've somehow internalized it and it'll come out' - knowledge integration through internalization rather than conscious memorization.

'Everyone was just so impressed by it, and I thought, I don't know, I don't care. It's not a skill... To me, that's not useful knowledge' when referring to a partner with photographic memory who could recall exact document locations.
Distinguishes between impressive recall abilities ('where a piece of paper was in a file from three years ago') and actually useful knowledge for problem-solving and decision-making.
Learn through internalization where good experiences become part of operating knowledge without conscious effort to recall specific sources or details.
properties.context: Knowledge work where synthesis and integration matter more than precise recall of sources and specific facts.

properties.description: Value knowledge based on its practical utility for problem-solving rather than its impressiveness or precision of recall.
properties.context: Professional environments where being able to recall specific details is less important than having internalized principles for decision-making.

properties.content: Dan worked with a partner who had 'at least at the time, we called it a photographic memory' and could recall exactly 'where a piece of paper was in a file from three years ago.' While 'everyone was just so impressed by it,' Dan thought 'I don't know, I don't care. It's not a skill... To me, that's not useful knowledge.'

When asked about leveraging specific content from reading, Dan identifies as closer to the 'amalgamation' approach: 'I just don't think I read. I don't even try to recall as much as if it was a good experience. Well, then I've somehow internalized it and it'll come out' naturally in relevant situations.

properties.description: 'I can't just keep trying to answer based on what I think my mental model is. I just have to answer it. If I go on a personal tangent, well, then I go on a personal tangent.' Authenticity requires abandoning preconceived self-narratives.

properties.id: Don't Try to Connect the Dots
properties.description: 'Don't try to connect the dots' - allowing natural responses rather than forcing coherent narratives during self-examination or conversation.

'I think I reframe much more than I realize, but I don't think of it as reframing. When I think about collaborating, I try to encourage someone to do something different, and I end up reframing issues a lot until I find the one that resonates with them. I didn't realize I did that.'
Continuously reframe issues during collaboration until finding the perspective that resonates with the other person, often without conscious awareness of doing so.
properties.context: Collaborative problem-solving where different people need different frames to understand and engage with the same underlying issue.

properties.description: Allow natural, authentic responses rather than trying to maintain consistency with preconceived self-understanding or desired image.
properties.context: Self-examination or coaching situations where discovery requires abandoning constructed narratives about oneself.

properties.content: Reflecting on the previous session, Dan realized 'I think I reframe much more than I realize, but I don't think of it as reframing. When I think about collaborating, I try to encourage someone to do something different, and I end up reframing issues a lot until I find the one that resonates with them. I didn't realize I did that.'

Dan emphasizes the importance of authentic response in interviews: 'I can't just keep trying to answer based on what I think my mental model is. I just have to answer it. If I go on a personal tangent, well, then I go on a personal tangent.' He advocates for not trying to 'connect the dots' but letting responses emerge naturally.

properties.description: 'I get through a little bit because of the authority conferred upon me, but that's not how I wanted it to happen.' Preferring genuine understanding over compliance through positional power.

'Continuing to reframe it from this, "This isn't what you have to do. This is what's right for the business." If you can save some time doing this, we can do this. This versus this is what you got to do because it's stupid.' Shifting from obligation/judgment to business value and opportunity.
Moving from complex automation to 'more cut and paste' solutions that are 'simpler for him' rather than insisting on optimal technical solutions.
Persistently reframe the same issue using different perspectives (business value, time savings, opportunity) until finding one that resonates with the person's motivations and comfort level.
properties.context: Change management situations where initial resistance requires finding alternative frames that align with the person's values and concerns.

properties.content: Dan worked with a warehouse manager who spends 'two hours every day' manually retyping customer information into FedEx because he's 'actually a little afraid of' computer technology. Instead of using authority or calling the process 'stupid,' Dan continuously reframed: 'This isn't what you have to do. This is what's right for the business. If you can save some time doing this, we can do this.' He adapted the solution to 'more cut and paste' to make it 'simpler for him.'

properties.description: 'Acting in the best interest of the business is the best way to act.' This represents a core mental model for decision-making that prioritizes business sustainability over other considerations.

'He tends to put the customer first, regardless of the financial implications... it's a balance. It's not always about the financial decision. It's not always about the customer. There's a balance that needs to be struck between it.' Business decisions require balancing competing priorities.
'I probably should say recognize, because he's not a... He's a bright guy.' The issue isn't intelligence or capability but awareness of principles already within reach.

'He doesn't ask more of himself or the team. I don't know. I don't know where I'd go with that. That's tougher.' Identifying the need for higher performance standards while acknowledging the difficulty of instilling this mindset.
Systematically work to help others 'recognize' (rather than learn) core business principles like business-first thinking and financial-customer balance.
properties.context: Leadership development where the goal is helping capable people adopt more sophisticated decision-making frameworks.

properties.description: Help people move from single-variable optimization (customer satisfaction) to multi-variable balancing (customer needs vs. financial reality).
properties.context: Business operations where employees naturally optimize for one factor but need to consider multiple competing priorities.

properties.content: Dan wants warehouse manager Brian to 'recognize' that 'acting in the best interest of the business is the best way to act.' Brian 'tends to put the customer first, regardless of the financial implications,' so Dan teaches balance: 'It's not always about the financial decision. It's not always about the customer. There's a balance that needs to be struck.' Dan also notes Brian 'doesn't ask more of himself or the team' but finds this harder to address.

properties.description: 'Everyone likes to run around saying, right people on the bus in the right seats. What has changed? A lot for me is you just need good people and give them direction. You don't need to spend as much time as you do trying to make sure there's an exact fit.'
'The right person in the right environment becomes self-managing over time if you allow it' - good people naturally adapt and become autonomous when given proper conditions.

'Every single time, I would throw out the tasks and I would write about the importance or the value because that's what will attract people.' Focus on meaning rather than specific duties in job descriptions.

'Critical thinking is everything. Business acumen is really important. If you get those right, you can put that person in almost any role and they'll do well.' These core capabilities matter more than specific skills.

'When I come across someone who relies on a bunch of skills tests to decide whether they want to hire the right person, I don't think that they've changed their odds of success at all.' Technical assessments don't predict success.
Hire for critical thinking and business acumen rather than exact role fit, trusting that good people will adapt and contribute quickly across various roles.
properties.context: Hiring decisions where flexibility and growth potential matter more than immediate technical skill match.

properties.description: Evaluate critical thinking capability during initial conversations rather than relying on formal testing or skills assessments.
properties.context: Hiring processes where identifying thinking quality is more important than measuring specific competencies.

properties.content: Dan's approach to hiring evolved from trying to find 'right people on the bus in the right seats' to believing 'you just need good people and give them direction.' When reviewing job descriptions 15-20 years ago, he would 'throw out the tasks and I would write about the importance or the value because that's what will attract people.'

Dan discovered the importance of critical thinking '10 or 15 years ago' and now believes 'critical thinking is everything. Business acumen is really important. If you get those right, you can put that person in almost any role and they'll do well.' He evaluates 'critical thinking in our first conversation' rather than using skills tests.

properties.description: 'My dad being self-employed was a factor. I think seeing a couple of brothers who own businesses was a factor.' These early exposures to entrepreneurship shaped fundamental perspectives on work and autonomy.

'I can get... I did get bored easily to the point where if I had the opportunity to break something, I would. That way, I had something else to do or to push just to go do something new.' Boredom drives destructive behavior to create new challenges.

'I view company life as pretty much a 12-month cycle, and not that much new happens year to year... You're doing the same shit every 12 months. You're just maybe doing it with more people, fewer people, bigger budget, smaller budget. You're still doing the same shit.'
'I need that phone to ring because it's nothing to do.' The requirement for external, unpredictable inputs to maintain engagement and energy.
When organizational work becomes predictable, intentionally create problems or disruptions to generate new challenges and maintain engagement.
properties.context: Corporate or structured environments where routine work cycles create understimulation for high-need-for-variety personalities.

properties.description: Require external, unpredictable inputs (like phone calls or new problems) to maintain energy and interest in work.
properties.context: Professional situations where internal motivation is insufficient and external stimulation is needed for sustained performance.

properties.content: Dan identifies formative influences as 'my dad being self-employed' and 'seeing a couple of brothers who own businesses' as factors that shaped his approach to work and business.

Dan describes getting 'bored easily to the point where if I had the opportunity to break something, I would. That way, I had something else to do or to push just to go do something new.' He views 'company life as pretty much a 12-month cycle' where 'not that much new happens year to year.'

When leaving Macy's for public accounting, a friend said 'I get why you left, but you are where you need to be.' This led to the realization 'I need that phone to ring because it's nothing to do' - recognizing the need for external stimulation and variety.

properties.description: When crisis hits, 'communicate through words or behavior that we're not looking at something that is the end of the world. It is important and it needs to be dealt with, but we're going to take a beat to make sure that we understand it and then move forward.'

Crisis flow state involves 'go into collaborator mode' where 'I'm not really head down trying to do it myself, but I'm trying to take in as much information as I can on the crisis.' For crises, 'it tends not to be directive.'
Immediately shift into 'collaborator mode' and rapidly solicit opinions from people and sources, prioritizing information intake over individual problem-solving.
properties.context: Acute crisis situations requiring immediate response, where collaborative intelligence gathering is more effective than individual analysis.

properties.description: First establish perspective that the crisis is manageable, then 'take a beat to make sure that we understand it' before moving into collaborative information gathering mode.
properties.context: High-pressure situations where team emotional regulation is crucial for effective crisis response.

properties.content: When a crisis happens on a Tuesday requiring immediate response, Dan's innate response is to first communicate that 'we're not looking at something that is the end of the world' while acknowledging its importance, then shift into collaborative mode to rapidly gather information rather than working alone.

properties.description: 'I go back to the financial foundation almost every day, whether I want to or not.' The accounting/CPA background provides constant practical value regardless of conscious intent to use it.

properties.id: Small Business Owner Knowledge Gap Recognition
properties.description: The accounting foundation is valuable 'because it's knowledge that most small business owners don't have.' This creates a consistent competitive advantage and value proposition.

Working at Arthur Anderson provided 'elevated status' in Cincinnati because 'if you worked there, you had an elevated status.' This early credibility foundation influences ongoing professional positioning.
Leverage financial and accounting knowledge as a daily, automatic resource that provides value even when not consciously deployed.
properties.context: Business consulting or advisory work where financial literacy provides consistent analytical advantage over business owners who lack this background.

properties.description: Use early association with prestigious organizations (like major accounting firms) to establish ongoing credibility and elevated status in professional relationships.
properties.context: Professional services where client confidence is influenced by past institutional affiliations and credentials.

properties.content: Dan identifies his 'master's in accounting, CPA, and working at a large public accounting CPA firm' as the foundation he returns to 'almost every day, whether I want to or not.' This knowledge is valuable 'because it's knowledge that most small business owners don't have.'

Working at Arthur Anderson, 'one of the largest firms in the world,' provided elevated status in Cincinnati where 'if you worked there, you had an elevated status,' establishing early credibility that influences ongoing professional positioning.

properties.id: Professional Circle Exposure as Learning Catalyst
properties.description: 'The exposure of working with various attorneys in thirty different states... you just get to know them, and you go out to dinner and things like that. You just learn a lot, not about law and taxes, but in everything. You learn from them.' This broad professional exposure creates knowledge beyond core competencies.

At the Limited, 'being a CPA wasn't that important... It was more about just taking that. I was making a lot of their judgments on appeals and litigation and everything. So it was more about judgment than anything versus advising a client.'

properties.id: Big Company Perspective as Small Business Advantage
properties.description: 'I can bring them a big company and big CPA firm perspective that they otherwise don't get.' The combination of large organization experience applied to small business contexts creates unique value.
Career progression from 'super specialist' at big CPA firm where 'I was a step removed from helping them' to Limited where 'I'm still a specialist, but I have greater responsibility.'
Actively absorb knowledge from diverse professional contacts beyond core technical areas, using social interactions to build broader perspective.
properties.context: Professional roles involving extensive interaction with experts from other fields, where relationship-building creates learning opportunities.

properties.description: Apply big company systems, perspectives, and judgment frameworks to small business contexts where such sophistication is typically unavailable.
properties.context: Consulting or advisory work with smaller organizations that lack access to enterprise-level thinking and processes.

properties.content: At the Limited, Dan gained 'exposure of working with various attorneys in thirty different states' and learning from them during dinners and social interactions. He notes 'you just learn a lot, not about law and taxes, but in everything' and that 'most attorneys are huge history buffs' who know their local history extensively.

Dan's career progression from large CPA firm specialist to Limited corporate role to local CPA firm allows him to 'bring them a big company and big CPA firm perspective that they otherwise don't get' when working with small businesses.

properties.name: Scaling Enterprise Discipline to Small Business

properties.description: 'The importance of moving your company toward professionalism and not just... I don't mean rigidity either, but I mean professionalism in the sense of a dedication that it's worth it, but it's really freaking heart. That's why they are where they are.'
properties.theme: Scaling Enterprise Discipline to Small Business

properties.description: Large organizations succeed through 'discipline that was non-negotiable for them.' Small businesses can adopt this discipline even without the same resources: 'we can't do it. We don't have the resources that they do. But they knew their numbers and they knew this and they knew that.'
properties.theme: Scaling Enterprise Discipline to Small Business

properties.description: At The Limited, 'individual divisions just running their own business' provides a model for small businesses: 'I know how this $500 million business ran. They ran their own.' This shows scalable principles regardless of size.
properties.theme: Scaling Enterprise Discipline to Small Business

properties.description: Extract the discipline and knowledge management practices from large organizations and adapt them for small business contexts, focusing on core principles rather than resource-dependent systems.
properties.theme: Scaling Enterprise Discipline to Small Business
properties.context: Small business consulting where introducing enterprise-level discipline around metrics, processes, and accountability can drive significant improvement.

properties.description: Use examples of how large company divisions operate independently to show small businesses that sophisticated business practices are achievable at their scale.
properties.theme: Scaling Enterprise Discipline to Small Business
properties.context: Situations where small business owners believe professional management practices are only for large companies.

properties.id: Limited Division Model for Small Business
properties.content: Dan uses his experience at The Limited, where 'individual divisions just running their own business' in a decentralized structure, to help small businesses. He tells them 'I know how this $500 million business ran. They ran their own. Yeah, we can't do it. We don't have the resources that they do. But they knew their numbers and they knew this and they knew that.' The key is adopting 'discipline that was non-negotiable for them.'
properties.theme: Scaling Enterprise Discipline to Small Business

properties.name: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility

properties.id: Being Right Isn't Always the Goal
properties.description: 'Heads and shoulders above all is... Being right isn't always the goal.' This represents a fundamental shift from rightness-based decision making to outcome-based flexibility.
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility

properties.description: Past approach was to 'base decisions and actions on what is right' which caused internal fury and detachment when things seemed wrong. This rigidity 'would just set me up to fail' and 'end up pissing her off because I wasn't doing it her way, even though it was wrong.'
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility

properties.description: 'I literally don't worry about it with clients anymore. They're go to do' what they want to do. This acceptance prevents the internal conflict that previously caused detachment and relationship damage.
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility

properties.description: Learning flexibility 'in part, for job security' represents a practical adaptation where survival required abandoning rigid righteousness in favor of relationship preservation.
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility

properties.description: Evolve from basing decisions on 'what is right' to accepting client preferences, even when they seem wrong, to preserve relationships and effectiveness.
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility
properties.context: Professional services where client relationships and outcomes matter more than being technically correct or morally superior.

properties.description: Avoid the cycle of internal fury and detachment that comes from focusing on rightness when working with less sophisticated decision-makers.
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility
properties.context: Working with business owners or leaders who lack technical expertise but have final decision authority.

properties.content: At the sawmill, owner Jo 'wasn't very sophisticated or understanding of business or finance' and 'would just want what she wanted.' Dan's insistence on doing what was 'right' would 'just set me up to fail' and 'end up pissing her off because I wasn't doing it her way, even though it was wrong.' This taught him flexibility over rigidity.
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility

properties.content: At The Limited, when Dan thought something was wrong, he 'would be furious internally, and it would cause me to lose interest for a period of time. I would almost become detached because I didn't want to have anything to do with it.' This pattern of rigidity became professionally limiting.
properties.theme: Evolution from Rigidity to Adaptive Flexibility

properties.description: Empathy wasn't needed at The Limited because 'everyone in our department, we were all the same, and they were very much black and white, but a big company. There's not a lot of gray.' But at the family sawmill 'they're gray all over the place' requiring empathy to manage effectively.

At the sawmill, managing people requires understanding they're 'in rural Indiana. They're not very well educated. They work hard as hell, but some of these guys are learnedly farmers. They've already been up five hours. So you have to put all that together when you're thinking about people's performance.'

'When you're working with any small business owner, one of the problems eventually becomes people. If your solution to everything is firearms or something like that, then you're not really helping them solve the problem.' Solutions must account for human complexity.
When asked to articulate his holistic approach as a soft skill, Dan states simply 'I am people-centered.'
Assess employee performance by integrating their full life context - education level, work ethic, background, and daily circumstances before work begins.
properties.context: Managing diverse workforces, particularly in rural or blue-collar environments where workers' backgrounds significantly impact their work performance and needs.

properties.description: Ensure business solutions account for human complexity rather than defaulting to simple disciplinary or systematic fixes.
properties.context: Small business consulting where people issues are inevitable and solutions must work with human nature rather than against it.

properties.content: At the family sawmill, Dan had to develop empathy because workers were 'in rural Indiana. They're not very well educated. They work hard as hell, but some of these guys are learnedly farmers. They've already been up five hours.' This required putting 'all that together when you're thinking about people's performance' - a stark contrast to The Limited where everyone was 'black and white.'

Dan explains that in small business consulting, 'one of the problems eventually becomes people. If your solution to everything is firearms or something like that, then you're not really helping them solve the problem.' When asked to name this soft skill, he identifies as 'people-centered.'

properties.description: 'Being a parent of three with now six grandchildren, it gives you a completely different perspective on things.' This family experience fundamentally alters how one approaches work and problems.

'What the grandkids serve as in effect is they're like the recharge vehicle, mental. I can take on other people's problems all day long and help as much as I can and produce data or whatever they want. But then, at the end of the day, if you stop by and see some of the kids, you're forced to comment on how pretty the dresses that they're wearing today is an exact copy from some Disney movie.'

'By moving all of your attention over there, even if it's for a short period of time, probably healthy, maybe keeps you more grounded.' The complete attention shift from business problems to simple, present-moment interactions with children provides psychological balance.
Use interactions with grandchildren to completely shift attention from complex business problems to simple, present-moment experiences like commenting on Disney dresses.
properties.context: High-stress professional work that requires periodic mental breaks and grounding through completely different types of human interaction.

properties.description: Leverage family relationships, particularly with grandchildren, as a systematic way to restore mental energy after taking on others' problems professionally.
properties.context: Consulting or advisory work where emotional and mental energy is constantly given to solve others' problems, requiring intentional restoration methods.

properties.content: Dan describes his six grandchildren as 'the recharge vehicle, mental' where after taking on 'other people's problems all day long,' stopping by to see the kids forces him to focus on simple things like 'how pretty the dresses that they're wearing today is an exact copy from some Disney movie.' This complete attention shift 'probably healthy, maybe keeps you more grounded.'

properties.id: Early Leadership Reality - Not Everyone Wants to be Led
properties.description: Class president experience taught 'at an early age... that you can't lead all people? Some people don't want to be led.' This fundamental leadership reality was learned through direct experience in high school.

As soccer coach, 'you're trying to figure out how to orchestrate this mess for the greater good. It wasn't for my greater good. It was really for the team's success.' Leadership focused on collective outcomes rather than personal benefit.

'If you're a coach and you're not a collaborator, I suspect that you're not very successful.' However, 'sometimes, you had to put your foot down and all that. So, that's that. That balance.' Leadership requires both collaborative and authoritative approaches.

As 'a freshman coach to 22 women, most of whom were older than me, it was quite telling' - learning to lead people with more experience and maturity created early lessons in authority without traditional credentials.
Consistently take on leadership roles from high school through college, creating situations where 'people relying on me' becomes a pattern.

properties.id: Profit as Managed Goal vs. Natural Result
properties.description: 'I do have a greater focus on profit than ever before because earlier, my focus was more about profit as a result, not something to be managed.' Evolution from passive to active profit management approach.

'I have realized that profit and cash are essentially the same thing. What is holding them back from their dreams, their employees' dreams, and just a better life is a lack of understanding of what it takes to create profit.'

'You're not going to hit a home run on any one of those areas and declare victory. You're always improving each one of those areas. That is what creates a better opportunity for profit.' No single breakthrough creates lasting profit improvement.
Better profit management 'relieves so much of the pressure that the owner is feeling' - profit isn't just financial but psychological relief.
Focus on continuously improving multiple profit drivers (revenue, expenses, taxes, etc.) rather than seeking breakthrough improvements in single areas.
properties.context: Small business consulting where sustainable profit improvement requires systematic attention to all contributing factors.

properties.description: Frame profit not as greed but as the enabler of 'dreams' for owners, employees, and better life quality, while providing psychological pressure relief.
properties.context: Working with business owners who may have conflicted feelings about profit-seeking or who undervalue profit management.

properties.id: Evolution from Profit as Result to Profit as Managed Goal
properties.content: Dan's approach has evolved to have 'greater focus on profit than ever before because earlier, my focus was more about profit as a result, not something to be managed.' He now realizes 'profit and cash are essentially the same thing' and that profit understanding is what enables 'their dreams, their employees' dreams, and just a better life.'

Dan's thinking evolved from fixating 'on just revenue, expenses, taxes, or something like that' to understanding 'it's much more complex to get there. You're not going to hit a home run on any one of those areas and declare victory. You're always improving each one of those areas' to create better profit opportunities.

properties.description: 'Not every sale is a good sale depending upon your business' - understanding that revenue growth must include customer selectivity and pricing strategy, not just volume.

'Most businesses don't pay enough attention to gross margin. They accept the price that they're charging because that's what they think the market allows, and their costs are their costs because the supplier has told them that's just what it is.'

'The real drivers are above the line more so than below the line. Any business can find 10% or 20% savings in overhead easily, but that's not driving your business anywhere. It's really about the revenue and the cost of sale.'
Businesses 'spend all their time trying to not by paper clips this month or cut back on supplies so that they could make their number' instead of focusing on major profit drivers.
Prioritize revenue optimization and cost of goods sold management over overhead reduction, recognizing that gross margin improvements drive business growth more than expense cutting.
properties.context: Small business profit improvement where owners often focus on easily visible overhead costs rather than more impactful revenue and direct cost management.

properties.description: Challenge accepted pricing and supplier costs rather than treating them as fixed constraints, actively managing gross margin as a key profit lever.
properties.context: Business situations where market positioning and supplier relationships can be renegotiated to improve profitability.

properties.content: Dan identifies key profit levers starting with 'revenue growth, which involves whether that is marketing, pricing, really understanding who your customer is' with the caveat that 'not every sale is a good sale.' He emphasizes that 'most businesses don't pay enough attention to gross margin' and focus too much on cutting overhead when 'the real drivers are above the line more so than below the line.'

Dan describes the common mistake where businesses 'spend all their time trying to not by paper clips this month or cut back on supplies so that they could make their number' when they should focus on 'revenue and the cost of sale.' While 'any business can find 10% or 20% savings in overhead easily... that's not driving your business anywhere.'

properties.description: 'You are achieving exactly the results you deserve... The market doesn't care. If you're afraid to raise your prices, you're achieving the results that you want.' Direct accountability for business outcomes through decision consequences.
'Most of it is within your control. Even the customers are within your control.' Rejecting victim mentality by emphasizing areas of business control and influence.

'Be as long as you're out there with a message of value and not what you do. You have a consistent message out there, you'll have customers.' Focus on value proposition rather than operational details.
Poor results stem from decision chains: afraid to raise prices, unwilling to enforce supplier accountability leading to missed shipping dates and lost customers - all controllable decisions.
Deliver direct, uncomfortable truths about business responsibility during planning sessions, linking current results directly to owner decisions and risk tolerance.
properties.context: Business planning sessions where owners need to accept responsibility for their role in creating current problems before solutions can be implemented.

properties.description: Redirect attention from external factors to areas within business control, including pricing decisions, supplier management, and customer communication.
properties.context: Business consulting where owners blame external factors rather than examining their own decision-making and control areas.

properties.content: Dan's most controversial perspective: standing 'in front of people and said, "Look, you are achieving exactly the results you deserve." That's pretty rough, but I do stand by it.' He explains this means if 'you're afraid to raise your prices, you're achieving the results that you want' and that 'most of it is within your control. Even the customers are within your control.'

Dan illustrates controllable decisions: 'If you're not willing, you'll miss a shipping date because someone else didn't do their job and get the materials in on time, and then the customer's pissed, and you lose the client. You're getting exactly the results that you deserve.' Success comes from having 'a message of value and not what you do' with 'a consistent message out there.'

properties.description: 'Because I've tried to do it within an organization instead of just talking about it.' Differentiation comes from having actually executed profit improvement strategies rather than just advising on them.

'I think I can give context better than most, and I think I can understand the impact on the business better than most. That's still a function of experience.' Context and impact understanding as core differentiators.

'Nothing's in isolation. Raising prices is a lot more than raising prices. It impacts others in the organization as well as the customer.' Rejecting simple cause-and-effect thinking in favor of systems impact analysis.

'Giving them context in that here is what it could mean and here is how you can go about it so that they understand the pluses and minuses versus... Look, if you increase prices 10%, you're going to make X. Well, it's just not that easy.'
Analyze profit improvement strategies through their interconnected effects on organization, customers, and implementation challenges rather than simple financial calculations.
properties.context: Business consulting where recommendations must account for real-world implementation complexities and organizational dynamics.

properties.description: Leverage direct implementation experience to provide realistic context about what profit strategies actually mean in practice, including challenges and unintended consequences.
properties.context: Consulting situations where clients need to understand not just what to do but how to do it and what to expect during implementation.

properties.content: When asked what makes him different from other profit consultants, Dan emphasizes 'Because I've tried to do it within an organization instead of just talking about it.' He believes he can 'give context better than most, and I think I can understand the impact on the business better than most' due to actual implementation experience.

Dan illustrates systems thinking with pricing: 'Nothing's in isolation. Raising prices is a lot more than raising prices. It impacts others in the organization as well as the customer.' He provides context about 'what it could mean and here is how you can go about it so that they understand the pluses and minuses versus... Look, if you increase prices 10%, you're going to make X. Well, it's just not that easy.'

properties.description: 'First, it's reading the room, and if I sense tension, then I don't go deep as quickly. I tend to stay on the surface and ask really easy questions.' This requires having advance knowledge of where tensions exist.

Address how different departments are 'stereotypically perceived' openly 'in front of everyone' to 'put everyone on the same level, that we are literally all in this together.' This involves speaking to how 'everyone else in the company is saying to them, even though I don't work there.'

Recognizing when groups are coming together 'for the first time they've ever done anything like that' or 'the first time they had really come together to talk about the future of the business' and treating these moments with appropriate significance.
Adjust the depth and pace of discussion based on sensed tension - stay surface-level with easy questions when tension is high, go deeper when the group is ready.
properties.context: Group planning sessions or team meetings where interpersonal or interdepartmental tensions may exist.

properties.description: Deliberately surface and acknowledge how different groups perceive each other stereotypically, addressing these perceptions openly to create equality and shared understanding.
properties.context: Cross-functional team sessions, particularly between traditionally conflicted departments like sales and operations.

properties.content: Dan achieves flow state leading planning sessions for companies, often their first time coming together beyond holiday parties to discuss business future. He starts with strengths/weaknesses, reads the room for tension, and proactively addresses sales/operations stereotypes by acknowledging how each group is typically perceived, creating a foundation of 'we are literally all in this together.'

properties.description: 'It's not an event... It was a series of small steps that added up to create a big impact.' Profit improvement happens through accumulated incremental changes rather than breakthrough moments.
'Because they don't know how businesses really work.' Deep operational understanding as the foundation for effective consulting, distinguishing from theoretical knowledge.

'Because they want to get paid for their big idea. And everyone who's inside an organization knows big ideas don't get implemented, they get killed.' Organizational reality that dramatic changes face resistance and failure.
The unique approach 'was natural. It evolved' - suggesting an organic, adaptive methodology rather than predetermined consulting frameworks.
Design and implement series of small, manageable changes that accumulate into significant business impact rather than pursuing dramatic transformations.
properties.context: Organizational change where resistance to big ideas requires a stealth approach through incremental improvements that don't trigger defensive reactions.

properties.description: Focus on how businesses actually operate rather than theoretical best practices, avoiding the consultant trap of selling dramatic ideas that won't be implemented.
properties.context: Business consulting where understanding operational reality and change capacity is more valuable than brilliant but impractical recommendations.

properties.content: When asked about his unique process, Dan describes it as 'natural. It evolved... a series of small steps that added up to create a big impact... It's not an event.' This incremental approach differs from other consultants because 'they don't know how businesses really work' and 'they want to get paid for their big idea. And everyone who's inside an organization knows big ideas don't get implemented, they get killed.'

properties.description: 'I give the owner confidence and clarity... It's strike that clarity then confidence. They have to have the clarity first of why they're doing it, because if there's this much hesitation, it gets blown up and whatever change that we agreed needs to happen.'
The investigation with phone logs and tracking 'was just confirming what he already knew' - providing data to support decisions they already sense need to be made.

'He knew he had to do it, he wanted to do it, but he didn't know how, which really was just saying I'm still nervous. Even though I have the clarity, I don't have the confidence yet.' Confidence comes from understanding the process, not just the need.
Spending 90 minutes on vacation to talk through the process until the owner was ready to act, resulting in 'He has not looked back since. He has felt no regret.'
Establish clear understanding of why a decision is necessary before building confidence in how to execute it, preventing hesitation from derailing implementation.
properties.context: Difficult business decisions where owners intellectually understand the need but lack emotional readiness to act.

properties.description: Invest significant time in process-focused conversations that build implementation confidence, even during personal time, to ensure decisive action.
properties.context: Critical business decisions where the cost of delayed or incomplete action exceeds the time investment in thorough preparation.

properties.content: Dan worked with a small company owner who struggled to fire an evasive customer service employee who avoided phone calls and worked remotely while 'riding his bike.' Despite evidence from phone logs and tracking, the owner 'knew he had to do it, he wanted to do it, but he didn't know how.' Dan spent '90 minutes' on vacation talking through the process until the owner had both clarity and confidence to act.

Dan's unique approach is giving owners 'confidence and clarity... It's strike that clarity then confidence. They have to have the clarity first of why they're doing it, because if there's this much hesitation, it gets blown up.' The sequence ensures that understanding the rationale precedes building courage to act.

properties.description: The effectiveness comes from being 'both a consultant and a friend, to a degree, or a confidant' - combining professional expertise with personal relationship depth.

properties.id: Focus and Clarity Over Clarity and Confidence
properties.description: 'I talk a lot about focus and clarity more so than clarity and confidence.' The more established framework emphasizes cognitive clarity and attention management.

properties.id: Medical Model of Stress as Framework
properties.description: References a 'medical model of stress' that he uses in presentations but doesn't often think about outside of presentation contexts.
'Part of, you know, me and why I'm such a horrible marketer' - only thinking about core frameworks during presentations rather than leveraging them for consistent marketing.
Only consciously access and articulate core frameworks when creating presentations, missing opportunities to use them consistently in marketing and daily practice.
properties.context: Professional development where valuable intellectual frameworks remain underutilized due to lack of systematic application beyond formal presentation contexts.

properties.description: Blend professional consulting expertise with personal relationship depth to provide both technical solutions and emotional support for difficult decisions.
properties.context: Professional services where technical competence alone is insufficient and clients need personal trust and emotional support to implement recommendations.

properties.id: Focus and Clarity vs. Clarity and Confidence
properties.content: When asked if 'clarity and confidence' is language he's used before, Dan clarifies 'I don't know that I've used it in that connection. I talk a lot about focus and clarity more so than clarity and confidence.' He references a 'medical model of stress' that he uses in presentations but admits he's 'such a horrible marketer' because he only thinks about these frameworks when presenting.

Mitch observes that Dan's effectiveness comes from being 'both a consultant and a friend, to a degree, or a confidant' - recognizing the human connection aspect as central to his consulting approach rather than purely technical expertise.

properties.description: 'The strategic planning session was not strategic planning. It was the identification of hurdles that are preventing us from moving forward. It was basically weaknesses.' Reframing strategic planning from visionary to problem-focused.

'Most of those companies did not even take that day, even as they left feeling really pumped up. They still didn't do much with that information. They didn't fix what needed to be fixed.' Emotional engagement doesn't translate to sustained action.

properties.id: Tiny Steps with No Backward Movement
properties.description: 'Any change at a small business is tiny steps. You just what you've got to do is just make sure none of those steps are backward. Sometimes it happens, but a small step forward is huge.' The focus is preventing regression while making minimal progress.

properties.id: Shiny Object Syndrome as Implementation Killer
properties.description: 'The mistake all the business owners make is they still go after the shiny red object because of everything it promises. That big marketing plan or that new marketing plan never gets fully implemented... that's why.' Large initiatives fail due to poor execution management.

'Anything can only be done in very small, incremental steps, the reason you don't read about that is from a marketing standpoint, that's not really very sexy, but it is reality. It is absolute reality.'
Focus exclusively on tiny, manageable steps while preventing backward movement, building momentum gradually over years rather than pursuing dramatic changes.
properties.context: Small business change management where capacity for change is limited and execution challenges kill large initiatives.

properties.description: Recognize that planning sessions create enthusiasm but don't guarantee implementation, requiring systematic follow-through and process management.
properties.context: Strategic planning situations where the gap between planning excitement and execution reality needs to be managed proactively.

properties.content: Dan's work with nonprofits doing strategic planning and advisory boards taught him that 'most of those companies did not even take that day, even as they left feeling really pumped up. They still didn't do much with that information.' Even a year later, 'they'd still be talking about the same damn things.' This cemented his belief that 'any change at a small business is tiny steps' focused on preventing backward movement.

Dan learned that business owners 'go after the shiny red object because of everything it promises. That big marketing plan... never gets fully implemented' due to poor execution. His conclusion: 'anything can only be done in very small, incremental steps' which 'from a marketing standpoint, that's not really very sexy, but it is reality. It is absolute reality.'

properties.description: 'No' - clients don't have access to the full strategic map because 'I just keep jumping around and don't really want to lay it out for...' The path is intentionally not revealed in its entirety.
The path to profitability is not linear, and next steps are determined dynamically: 'Very much' figuring out the next step while in the current step, informed by deeper business understanding.

'Marketers love to have these discovery sessions, which are 90 minutes of bullshit because all you're hearing is the owner's perspective of the business. That's not how things get done.' Formal discovery processes provide limited real insight.

'I end up learning more about how things really get done than the owner in many times, so it's hard for me to know what the next step is until I understand the business better.' Operational reality differs from owner perception.
'I don't know, experience' combined with understanding 'how things really get done' guides next step selection without predetermined roadmaps.
Keep the full strategic path hidden while providing clear rationale for individual steps, allowing for dynamic adaptation based on emerging understanding.
properties.context: Complex organizational change where revealing the full scope might create resistance or where the path genuinely needs to adapt based on discovered realities.

properties.description: Learn how the business actually operates through direct observation and employee interaction rather than relying on owner descriptions during formal discovery sessions.
properties.context: Business consulting where owner perceptions often differ significantly from operational reality, requiring independent investigation.

properties.content: When asked if clients see the full strategic map, Dan says 'No' because 'I just keep jumping around and don't really want to lay it out.' Instead, he explains each step as 'This is step one that will help us achieve your goal, but it is only one step. There might be 20 steps in between, there might be ten' without revealing the complete path.

Dan determines next steps through 'experience' informed by 'understanding the business better.' He criticizes 'discovery sessions, which are 90 minutes of bullshit because all you're hearing is the owner's perspective' and notes 'I end up learning more about how things really get done than the owner in many times.'

properties.name: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking

properties.id: Critical Thinking as Information Reception Plus Processing
properties.description: 'Critical thinking... is the ability to accept information and connect the dots for decision-making. So, what is really interesting about critical thinking is how you receive information is just as important as how you process it.'
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking

properties.description: 'His filter was so pronounced that we could sit next to each other and hear someone speak, and we would hear things completely differently... his filter caused him to hear things that are always negatively and things that could always go wrong.'
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking

properties.description: Optimal information reception is 'probably 80% objective and 20% subjective' - mostly accepting information as provided while maintaining some personal filter.
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking

properties.description: Good information receivers have 'a very strong emotional intelligence. So they're not reacting right away. They're willing to accept and process or hear it and process it before they accept it rather than just react.'
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking

properties.description: Evaluate how people receive information before assessing their processing abilities, looking for filters that distort input before analysis begins.
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking
properties.context: Hiring or team evaluation where decision-making quality depends on the ability to receive information accurately before processing it.

properties.description: Practice receiving information, processing it internally, then responding rather than immediate reaction, requiring strong emotional intelligence to manage initial impulses.
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking
properties.context: High-stakes decision-making environments where immediate reactions can lead to poor choices based on filtered or emotionally distorted information.

properties.content: Dan worked with a company president whose 'filter is so pronounced that there's a filter embedded with this trepidation over anything new.' This caused them to 'hear things completely differently' when sitting together - the president's filter 'caused him to hear things that are always negatively and things that could always go wrong.' Result: 'in two years, he was president, he never made a good decision. He couldn't because he couldn't hear it.'
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking

properties.id: Critical Thinking Definition and Reception Importance
properties.content: Dan defines critical thinking as 'the ability to accept information and connect the dots for decision-making' but emphasizes that 'how you receive information is just as important as how you process it.' Optimal reception is '80% objective and 20% subjective' with 'very strong emotional intelligence' to avoid immediate reactions.
properties.theme: Information Reception and Processing in Critical Thinking

properties.id: Connecting Dots as Critical Thinking Result
properties.description: 'Connecting the dots to me ends up being the result' of critical thinking, not the process itself. It represents the synthesis outcome rather than the method.

When sales decline despite adding staff, poor critical thinking leads to 'fire the first salesperson, or maybe you fire all the salespeople because it's always binary and it's anything but binary. Whereas if you employ critical thinking, then you are naturally doing much more investigation to understand the problem.'

properties.id: Modified Socratic Method as Toolbox Item
properties.description: 'I don't think of it as... It might be natural, but I don't know that about instinct as much as it's in my toolbox. It is a modification of the Socratic method. It's really all that it is. We're just trying to ask a question in response to your first question.'

'The intention of the questioning is to figure out where the person's coming from. So, yeah, their assumptions, what caused them to say what they just said?' Focus on understanding reasoning behind statements.
Use modified Socratic questioning to understand the assumptions and reasoning that led to someone's conclusion, avoiding binary reactions in favor of deeper investigation.
properties.context: Problem-solving situations where initial explanations may be oversimplified and require deeper understanding of underlying assumptions.

properties.description: Synthesize multiple layers of relevant data rather than accepting surface-level explanations or jumping to binary solutions.
properties.context: Business problem-solving where complex issues require understanding multiple contributing factors rather than single-cause explanations.

properties.content: When a business owner says 'Our sales declined 10% last year. By the way, we added another person to the sales staff,' poor critical thinking leads to binary solutions like firing salespeople. Good critical thinking employs 'much more investigation to understand the problem' rather than jumping to simple cause-and-effect conclusions.

properties.id: Modified Socratic Method as Critical Thinking Tool
properties.content: Dan describes his critical thinking approach as 'a modification of the Socratic method' where the goal is 'trying to ask a question in response to your first question.' The intention is 'to figure out where the person's coming from... their assumptions, what caused them to say what they just said?'

properties.name: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods

properties.description: 'One of the tools that I use very consciously is repetition... I'm pretty sure the next time that issue comes around, they're not going to remember... So I keep coming back and saying, "Okay, now, remember what we talked about last week?"'
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods

properties.description: 'I can't turn someone into a strong critical thinker.' Acknowledging the fundamental limitation that critical thinking ability has natural boundaries that coaching cannot overcome.
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods

properties.description: 'Break it up into as many parts as you can and put in some check-in points along the way to where you're literally just checking their thinking... Like, stop. Don't do this until you've checked with me.'
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods

properties.description: 'That doesn't feel right, and here's why it doesn't feel right. So, if you have some facts that will change my mind, I'm very open to it, but until then, I'm not there... What can you do to bring me some facts to help me understand where you are?'
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods

properties.description: Deliberately repeat important thinking patterns and conclusions to help people remember and apply them to similar future situations.
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods
properties.context: Working with team members who struggle to transfer learning from one situation to similar situations without explicit reinforcement.

properties.description: Break complex decisions into smaller parts with check-in points, allowing guided thinking without taking over the domain expertise role.
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods
properties.context: Situations where you need to improve someone's thinking process but cannot directly solve their technical problems due to lack of domain knowledge.

properties.description: Use intuitive sense that something 'doesn't feel right' to challenge thinking, then require the person to provide facts that address the concern.
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods
properties.context: Coaching situations where you sense flawed reasoning but cannot directly identify the technical errors due to domain limitations.

properties.content: Dan uses 'repetition' consciously because when people reach conclusions through guided thinking, 'the next time that issue comes around, they're not going to remember... They're not going to go back and connect the dots again.' So he keeps 'coming back and saying, "Okay, now, remember what we talked about last week?"'
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods

properties.content: When working with poor critical thinkers in domains where he lacks expertise, Dan says 'that doesn't feel right, and here's why it doesn't feel right. So, if you have some facts that will change my mind, I'm very open to it, but until then, I'm not there, so we can't move forward.' He pushes responsibility back: 'What can you do to bring me some facts to help me understand where you are?'
properties.theme: Critical Thinking Development and Support Methods

properties.description: 'I will often come to an instant conclusion. But I know that I don't act on it. So, I may have a thought, but I don't... I don't express it typically because I'm still in the mode of just gathering more, so I do not act a lot on intuition.'

Intuition operates at the process level in crisis situations where 'there's no plan in front of you.' It guides whether to 'blur out something and solve the problem' or recognize 'I need to get more information, and I need these people to... I need someone else to help me make this decision.'
Allow instant conclusions to form while maintaining discipline to not express or act on them immediately, staying in information-gathering mode instead.
properties.context: Crisis or complex decision-making situations where first instincts may be valuable but premature action could be harmful.

properties.description: Use intuition to determine the appropriate decision-making process - whether to act quickly on a solution or shift into collaborative information-gathering mode.
properties.context: Unplanned crisis situations where there's 'no plan in front of you' and the process itself must be intuitively selected.

properties.content: In crisis situations without a plan, Dan describes intuition as having two potential paths: 'It could be blur out something and solve the problem. Or your intuition could be, I need to get more information, and I need these people to... I need someone else to help me make this decision.' The intuition guides process selection rather than direct answers.

properties.description: 'You can teach critical thinking... But if you're lousy, you can't become excellent. You can improve.' There are natural limits to how much critical thinking ability can be developed through training.

properties.id: Poor Critical Thinking as Dot Connection Failure
properties.description: 'To me, it's an inability to connect the dots' combined with drawing 'incorrect conclusions based upon either inferring facts which aren't there or based on emotion.'
'I think of problem-solving as a subset of critical thinking skills' because critical thinking has broader applications beyond specific problem-solving contexts.

Critical thinking 'enables you to go through an election season and not get crazy from the ads. Because the left is as full of shit as the right... I don't act on it because they haven't given me enough information to draw the conclusion they want me to draw.'
Distinguish between drawing conclusions based on actual evidence versus inferring facts that aren't present or making emotion-based judgments.
properties.context: Decision-making situations where incomplete information or emotional pressure can lead to false conclusions.

properties.description: Evaluate whether provided information is sufficient to support the conclusions being promoted, maintaining immunity to persuasion when evidence is inadequate.
properties.context: Media consumption, advertising, or persuasive communications where the goal is to influence behavior without providing complete information.

properties.content: Dan acknowledges 'You can teach critical thinking. I've done it. I taught a short course on critical thinking' to explain what it is and why it's important. However, 'if you're lousy, you can't become excellent. You can improve' - there are natural ceilings to development.

Dan sees critical thinking as broader than problem-solving, enabling you to 'go through an election season and not get crazy from the ads. Because the left is as full of shit as the right. It's just an ad... I don't act on it because they haven't given me enough information to draw the conclusion they want me to draw.'

properties.name: Critical Thinking as Balanced Umbrella Skill

properties.description: 'If you have high critical thinking skills, you are a problem solver. But it's not just about solving problems. It's just how you look at things.' Critical thinking encompasses multiple cognitive abilities including problem-solving.
properties.theme: Critical Thinking as Balanced Umbrella Skill

properties.id: Emotional Intelligence as Critical Thinking Component
properties.description: 'I'm tempted to put emotional intelligence under there. I'd probably have to think about that one a little bit longer, though.' This represents an unconventional but potentially valid connection.
properties.theme: Critical Thinking as Balanced Umbrella Skill

properties.description: 'Too much critical thinking could get in the way because your logic brain is shutting down too much of the "what if"... moonshot goals probably don't sit well with a critical thinker because I can't envision it, but I certainly can't figure out how to get there.'
